title: Paper 1 Questions 1 and 2: finding information and analysing language
specPoints: Paper 1 Section A: Question 1 (AO1, 4 marks) and Question 2 (AO2, 8 marks)

tips.title: Fifteen minutes before the pen
tips.body: The paper advises about 15 minutes reading the source and all five questions before writing. Two reads of the text, the second with a pencil, then the questions; that is what makes Question 3 and Question 4 possible later.

tips.title: Four tests for a Question 1 point
tips.body: About the subject; from the given lines; true; separate. If you can put the subject's name in front of the point and it makes sense, it passes the first test. An inference the lines do not make fails the third.

tips.title: Choice, effect, why
tips.body: Name the writer's choice, give its effect on the reader, then say why the words produce it. The third move is where Level 3 becomes Level 4, and it is the one most answers leave out.

tips.title: One simile, four levels
tips.body: The June 2024 scheme climbed its whole ladder on the lizards darting like flames: what the word means, what the image suggests, what it shows about the heat, what it does to the reader's sense of the character. Same detail, deeper each time.

tips.title: Inside the lines, or the ceiling is Level 2
tips.body: Question 2 is marked on the lines the question prints. An answer that writes only about language from elsewhere in the source is placed in Level 1 or 2 however brilliant it is.

tips.title: Sentence forms are choices too
tips.body: An exclamation, a short plain statement, a long sentence held open by dashes, a sentence that corrects itself: name the shape and say what it does. It is the third bullet under the question and the one that most separates strong answers.

why.matters: Reading closely is the skill under every other skill in English: seeing that a writer chose this word, this image, this shape of sentence, and asking what the choice does. Paper 1 tests it directly, four marks for finding what is there and eight for explaining how the language works, and it tests it again, less directly, in the two bigger questions that follow and in the writing task, where the student becomes the one making the choices. The habit of asking why a word is there is also how a reader gets more out of any book, article or speech than someone who takes the words as given.

examples.title: Reading a text that wants something from you
examples.body: An advertisement, a political leaflet and a charity appeal all choose their words to make a reader feel before the reader has thought. The person who can name the choice, a simile that makes a product feel like weather, a short sentence placed for weight, a list that builds a mood, can see the work being done and decide whether to be moved by it. That is Question 2 applied to the world outside the exam.

examples.title: The 15 minutes a lawyer or a doctor spends reading
examples.body: A contract, a witness statement and a set of clinical notes are all read the way the paper asks the source to be read: once for what they say, once with a pencil for exactly which words carry the weight. The rule for Question 1, only what is in the lines and no inference the text does not make, is the rule those readers work by, because a guess dressed as a fact is what goes wrong in their trades.

steps.title: Paper 1 in one look
steps.body:
Paper 1 is 1 hour 45 minutes and 80 marks, half the GCSE. It comes with an insert: one prose fiction extract from the 20th or 21st century, about a page long, with the lines numbered. Section A asks four questions about it, worth 40 marks; Section B asks for one piece of creative writing, worth 40.

The front of the paper advises about 15 minutes reading the source and all five questions, about 45 minutes on Section A and about 45 on Section B. That advice is the plan.

**The four reading questions rise in size.** Question 1 is 4 marks and takes a few minutes. Question 2 is 8 marks on a short passage. Question 3 is 8 marks on the whole text. Question 4 is 20 marks, half of Section A, on the second part of the text. This topic covers the first two; the next two topics take one question each.

rows: List four things about …
A few given lines
How does the writer use language here to …
A passage of about ten lines
How has the writer structured the text?
The whole source
To what extent do you agree?
The second part of the source
Write a description or a story
A choice of two tasks

steps.title: Question 1: list four things
steps.body:
Question 1 names a few lines and a subject and asks for four things. In June 2024 it was lines 1 to 6 and four things about Mary. One mark for each point, and the mark scheme's rules are exact.

**What counts.** A point must come from the given lines only. It can be a quotation or a paraphrase; a single word is enough and full sentences are not required. It must be true, and it must be about the subject named: the scheme rejected anything about the setting that did not include Mary. An answer that combines two correct points in one line is given both marks.

**What the examiners ask themselves**, in the scheme's own words: does it tell you something about her; is it from the correct section; is it true; and if you put her name in front of it, does it make sense.

**What loses marks.** A point from later in the text. An inference the lines do not support: *she was tired* and *she was dehydrated* were rejected when the text said her head ached and she wanted water. Something that is in the lines but is not about her.

props.centre: The four tests for a Question 1 point

boxes.title: About the subject?
boxes.body: Would it make sense with her name in front?

boxes.title: From the lines?
boxes.body: Only the lines the question gives

boxes.title: True?
boxes.body: In the text, not inferred beyond it

boxes.title: Separate?
boxes.body: Four different points, or two in one line

visuals.alt: Four boxes giving the four tests a Question 1 point must pass: about the subject, from the given lines, true, and separate

check.prompt: June 2024 asked for four things about Mary from lines 1 to 6, where the text says her head ached and she went to get a glass of water. Which answer would the mark scheme reject?
check.solution: *She was dehydrated* is an inference the lines do not make: they say her head ached and she wanted water, which is not the same. The scheme accepted *her head ached*, *she went to get a glass of water* and *she was unwell*, and rejected *she was dehydrated* and *she was tired*. Question 1 rewards what is there, not what might follow from it.

markScheme.description: She was dehydrated

options: She was unwell
Her head ached
She was dehydrated
She went to get a glass of water

steps.title: The practice text: the opening of Miss Brill
steps.body:
The extracts in this unit come from Katherine Mansfield's short story *Miss Brill*, published in 1920, which is out of copyright and can be printed in full. A woman goes alone to a public garden on a Sunday afternoon, as she does every week, to listen to the band and watch the people. This is the opening.

> Although it was so brilliantly fine—the blue sky powdered with gold and great spots of light like white wine splashed over the Jardins Publiques—Miss Brill was glad that she had decided on her fur. The air was motionless, but when you opened your mouth there was just a faint chill, like a chill from a glass of iced water before you sip, and now and again a leaf came drifting—from nowhere, from the sky. Miss Brill put up her hand and touched her fur. Dear little thing! It was nice to feel it again. She had taken it out of its box that afternoon, shaken out the moth-powder, given it a good brush, and rubbed the life back into the dim little eyes. "What has been happening to me?" said the sad little eyes. Oh, how sweet it was to see them snap at her again from the red eiderdown!... But the nose, which was of some black composition, wasn't at all firm. It must have had a knock, somehow. Never mind—a little dab of black sealing-wax when the time came—when it was absolutely necessary.... Little rogue! Yes, she really felt like that about it. Little rogue biting its tail just by her left ear. She could have taken it off and laid it on her lap and stroked it. She felt a tingling in her hands and arms, but that came from walking, she supposed. And when she breathed, something light and sad—no, not sad, exactly—something gentle seemed to move in her bosom.

> There were a number of people out this afternoon, far more than last Sunday. And the band sounded louder and gayer. That was because the Season had begun. For although the band played all the year round on Sundays, out of season it was never the same. It was like some one playing with only the family to listen; it didn't care how it played if there weren't any strangers present. Wasn't the conductor wearing a new coat, too? She was sure it was new. He scraped with his foot and flapped his arms like a rooster about to crow, and the bandsmen sitting in the green rotunda blew out their cheeks and glared at the music. Now there came a little "flutey" bit—very pretty!—a little chain of bright drops. She was sure it would be repeated. It was; she lifted her head and smiled.

Read it twice: once for what happens, once with a pencil for anything that catches. That is what the 15 minutes at the start of the paper are for.

rows: What is happening and to whom
Mark words, images and sentence shapes that stand out
Read all five questions
Where the text moves: outside to inside, now to then
Note where the mood changes
Find the lines each question names

visuals.alt: A table of the two reads of the source and what to do after them: the first for what happens, the second with a pencil, then the questions

check.prompt: Question 1 asks: list four things about Miss Brill from the first four sentences of the extract. Which of these is a point the mark scheme would accept?
check.solution: *She was glad that she had decided on her fur* is in the opening sentence and is about her. The band is later in the text and not about her; the honey-cake is at the end of the story; *she was feeling cold* is an inference the text does not make, since it says only that there was a faint chill in the air. Only the point about the fur passes all four tests.

options: She bought a slice of honey-cake at the baker's

steps.title: Question 2: how does the writer use language here
steps.body:
Question 2 prints a passage of about ten lines and asks how the writer uses language to do something: in June 2024, to describe the effects of the heat. Three bullets name the ground: the writer's choice of words and phrases, language features and techniques, and sentence forms. Eight marks, AO2.

**Four levels.** Level 1, 1 to 2 marks: simple, limited comment. Level 2, 3 to 4: some understanding and comment. Level 3, 5 to 6: clear, relevant explanation. Level 4, 7 to 8: perceptive, detailed analysis, which the scheme describes as analysing the effects of the writer's choices, selecting a range of judicious textual detail, and making sophisticated and accurate use of terminology.

**The same detail at four levels.** The June 2024 scheme shows the ladder on one simile, the heat lizards that “darted over the rocks like flames”. At Level 1 the comment says the word *flames* tells us they were hot and *darted* shows they are fast. At Level 2 it says the heat is so strong the lizards cannot stay still. At Level 3 it explains that the simile suggests the heat is reflected in the wildlife and the verb creates the lizards' rapid movement. At Level 4 the analysis reads the imagery as the lizards transforming into fire, conveying the character's perception of the heat's power to change nature, and the verb as extending that image.

The detail did not change. What changed was how far the comment went: from what the word means, to what it suggests, to what it does to the reader's sense of the whole.

rows: 1: simple, limited
Flames tells us they were hot; darted shows they are fast
2: some understanding
The heat is so strong the lizards cannot stay still
3: clear, relevant
The simile shows the heat reflected in the wildlife; the verb creates rapid movement
4: perceptive, detailed
Lizards transforming into fire convey her sense of the heat changing nature; the verb extends the image
props.title: One simile, four levels

visuals.alt: A table of the four levels of Question 2, with the June 2024 mark scheme's comments on one simile at each level

check.prompt: What separates the Level 4 comment from the Level 3 comment on the same simile?
check.solution: Both levels name the simile and the verb. The Level 4 comment goes further into effect: the lizards become fire, and that is how the character perceives the heat's power. Depth of analysis on a well-chosen detail, not more terms or more quotations, is the difference the scheme shows.

markScheme.description: Level 4 reads the image as a transformation and connects it to the character's perception, where Level 3 explains what the simile shows

options: Level 4 reads the image as a transformation and connects it to the character's perception, where Level 3 explains what the simile shows
Level 4 uses more technical terms than Level 3, which is what the descriptor means by sophisticated and accurate use of subject terminology
Level 4 writes about more quotations than Level 3, since a range of detail means at least five
Level 4 says the simile is effective and Level 3 does not, and the examiners want a judgement

steps.title: Building a Level 4 paragraph on Miss Brill
steps.body: Suppose the question is: how does the writer use language to show how Miss Brill feels about her fur? Here is one paragraph built the way the scheme rewards.

visuals.problem: Choose a detail, name the choice, give its effect, and say why the words produce it.

steps.text: Choose: the fur has “dim little eyes” into which Miss Brill has “rubbed the life back”, and it is a “Dear little thing!”
steps.note: Two details that work together beat two that do not. Both make the fur alive.

steps.text: Name the choice: the fur is personified, and the exclamation is her own voice breaking into the narration.
steps.note: Terminology that does work: personification, exclamatory sentence, free indirect style.

steps.text: Give the effect: the reader sees a woman talking to an object as if it were a pet, and feels how little else she has to talk to.
steps.note: Effect on the reader, not just on the sentence.

steps.text: Say why: *rubbed the life back* is what you do to a numb hand or a cold creature, so the fur is something she revives each Sunday; the eyes are *dim* until she attends to them, as she is until the band plays.
steps.note: The words themselves explain the effect. This is what analysis means.

steps.text: Extend: the “Little rogue!” biting its tail is a second exclamation, playful this time, so the fur is a companion with a character of its own.
steps.note: A second detail extends the first rather than starting again.

boxes.title: Choose
boxes.body: A detail worth the time; two that connect

boxes.title: Effect
boxes.body: On the reader, not on the sentence

boxes.title: Why
boxes.body: How the words themselves produce it

visuals.alt: Four boxes for a Level 4 paragraph: choose a detail, name the choice, give its effect, and say why the words produce it

check.prompt: Which comment on the words rubbed the life back into the dim little eyes is analysis rather than feature-spotting?
check.solution: The comment about the numb hand and the fur revived each Sunday names the choice and explains the effect through the words themselves, then connects it to the character. The comment that defines personification adds a stock phrase; the one about adjectives and alliteration labels parts of speech; the one about the box and the money is a plot inference. Only the comment about reviving the fur is the analysis of effect the top level asks for.

markScheme.description: The verb phrase is what you do to a numb hand or a cold creature, so the fur becomes something Miss Brill revives each Sunday, as the band revives her

options: The writer uses personification here, which is when an object is given human qualities, and this makes the description more vivid and interesting for the reader to picture
The verb phrase is what you do to a numb hand or a cold creature, so the fur becomes something Miss Brill revives each Sunday, as the band revives her
The word dim is an adjective and eyes is a noun, and the phrase uses alliteration on the letter l in little and life
This shows that the fur is old and has been in a box, which tells us that Miss Brill does not have much money

steps.title: Sentence forms: the bullet most answers skip
steps.body:
The third bullet under Question 2 is sentence forms, and the scheme's own examples use it: the June 2024 indicative content for Question 4 noted the short, exclamatory *Listen to me!* set against an attempt to keep calm. A sentence form is a choice like any other.

**In the opening of Miss Brill.** The first sentence is long and winding, held open by dashes, and it takes the reader through the sky, the light and the gardens before arriving at her decision about the fur: the sentence does what the afternoon does. Then the short ones: “Dear little thing!” and “Little rogue!” are exclamations in her own voice. “It must have had a knock, somehow.” is a plain statement that ends on a shrug. And the paragraph closes on a sentence that corrects itself mid-way, “something light and sad—no, not sad, exactly—something gentle”, where the dashes show a feeling being adjusted as it is felt.

**How to write about it.** Name the form, say what it does, and tie it to the meaning: *the exclamation lets her voice break into the narration, so the reader hears her as she hears herself.*

rows: A long sentence held open by dashes
The first sentence, sky to fur
Takes the reader on the wandering afternoon
Exclamation
Dear little thing! Little rogue!
Her own voice breaks in; the fur is a companion
A short plain statement
It must have had a knock, somehow.
A shrug; she will not look at the damage
Self-correction with dashes
sad—no, not sad, exactly—something gentle
A feeling adjusted as it is felt
props.title: Four sentence forms

visuals.alt: A table of four sentence forms in the opening of Miss Brill with what each does

check.prompt: What does the self-correcting sentence, something light and sad—no, not sad, exactly—something gentle, do?
check.solution: The sentence changes its mind in the middle, and the dashes let the reader see the change. Miss Brill reaches for *sad*, will not have it, and settles on *gentle*: the form performs her refusal to admit the feeling. That is a sentence-form point with an effect attached.

markScheme.description: It shows a feeling being adjusted as it is felt, so the reader watches Miss Brill refuse the word sad

options: It shows that the writer could not decide which of the two words to use and so left both of them in the sentence
It uses dashes, which are a form of punctuation that makes the sentence longer
It shows a feeling being adjusted as it is felt, so the reader watches Miss Brill refuse the word sad
It tells the reader that Miss Brill is happy, because gentle is a positive word

steps.title: Two more details from the opening
steps.body:
Take each of these and write the four moves: choose, name, effect, why.

1. “like a chill from a glass of iced water before you sip”
2. “He scraped with his foot and flapped his arms like a rooster about to crow”

For the first, ask why the writer chose a glass of water rather than a cold wind; for the second, ask what the comparison to a rooster does to the conductor, and to the woman watching him. Then read the two paragraphs again and choose the detail you would most want to write about under exam conditions, with the reason.

boxes.title: Why this word?
boxes.body: What would a plainer word have lost?

boxes.title: Why this image?
boxes.body: What does the comparison bring with it?

boxes.title: Why this shape?
boxes.body: What does the sentence form do?

boxes.title: So what?
boxes.body: What does the reader now feel or see?

visuals.alt: Four boxes of questions to ask any detail: why this word, why this image, why this shape, and so what

check.prompt: What does the simile like a rooster about to crow do to the conductor?
check.solution: A rooster about to crow is puffed up and pleased with itself, and the simile lets the reader share the amused, affectionate eye of the watcher. The detail characterises Miss Brill as much as the conductor, which is why it is worth writing about.

markScheme.description: It makes him faintly comic and self-important, seen through the eyes of a woman who enjoys watching people

options: It shows that the band is playing badly, because a rooster is a noisy and unmusical bird and the conductor looks like one
It tells the reader that the concert is taking place early in the morning, when roosters crow
It suggests that the conductor is angry with the bandsmen and is about to shout at them
It makes him faintly comic and self-important, seen through the eyes of a woman who enjoys watching people

steps.title: Judicious: choosing what to write about
steps.body:
The Level 4 descriptor asks for a range of judicious textual detail. Judicious means chosen with judgement: not the three things found soonest, but the details that best answer the question and that connect.

**Read the question's focus first.** *How does the writer use language here to describe the effects of the heat* wants details about the heat's effects, not the best-written sentence in the passage. In June 2024 the scheme's own examples were an image of heat-waves beating up from stone and the lizards like flames: both effects, both violent movement, and the second extends the first.

**Choose details that build.** Two details that make one point in two ways earn more than four that make four points in one line each. The fur's dim eyes and the exclamation over it are one idea, a companion; the long first sentence and the self-correcting last one are one idea, a mind wandering and adjusting.

**Terminology sophisticated and accurate.** *Personification*, *free indirect style*, *exclamatory sentence* are worth using when they are right; *the writer uses adjectives* is accurate and worth nothing. A term earns when it names a choice the reader would otherwise miss.

**Stay inside the lines.** The scheme places an answer that writes only about language outside the given lines in Level 1 or 2 however good it is.

boxes.title: Focused
boxes.body: Details that answer the question asked

boxes.title: Connected
boxes.body: Two that make one point beat four that make four

boxes.title: Exact
boxes.body: A term that names a choice, not a label

boxes.title: Inside the lines
boxes.body: Outside them, the ceiling is Level 2

visuals.alt: Four boxes on judicious detail: focused on the question, connected, named exactly, and from inside the given lines

check.prompt: A Question 2 passage is about a character's fear. Which choice of details is judicious?
check.solution: Judicious means chosen for the question and for how they connect. Striking phrases off the focus, one per line, or a detail from outside the given lines all fail the descriptor, and the detail from outside the lines carries a ceiling of Level 2.

markScheme.description: Two details that both build the fear, one an image and one a sentence form, analysed for how they work together

options: Two details that both build the fear, one an image and one a sentence form, analysed for how they work together
One quotation from every line of the passage, so that the whole passage is covered
The best simile in the whole source, even though it is outside the given lines, because it is the best
The four most striking phrases in the passage, whatever they happen to be about, each with a technique named and a comment on it

steps.title: Questions 1 and 2 in one page
steps.body:
The first two questions are worth twelve marks and take about fifteen minutes between them. They reward exactness.

- **Read for 15 minutes:** twice through the source, then all five questions, before writing.
- **Question 1, 4 marks:** four separate true things about the named subject, from the given lines only; a word will do; no inferences beyond the text.
- **Question 2, 8 marks:** only the given lines; words and phrases, features and techniques, sentence forms; the ladder runs from what a word means to what it suggests to what it does to the reader.
- **The Level 4 move:** choose a judicious detail, name the choice exactly, give the effect on the reader, and say why the words produce it; let a second detail extend the first.
- **Sentence forms count:** an exclamation, a short plain sentence, a long one held open by dashes, a sentence that corrects itself.

Everything here is practised on Mansfield's *Miss Brill*, which the next two topics follow to its ending.

rows: Four true things, from the lines, about the subject
An inference the text does not make
Choice, effect, why, inside the lines
Naming a technique with no effect; leaving the lines

check.prompt: How many marks is Question 2 worth?
check.solution: Eight marks, for AO2, on a passage of about ten lines. Question 1 is four, Question 3 is eight and Question 4 is twenty, which makes forty for Section A.

questions.prompt: How many marks is Question 1 worth?
questions.solution: 4 marks: one for each thing listed, from the given lines, about the named subject. It is the smallest question on the paper and should take only a few minutes.

questions.prompt: Which kind of text is the Paper 1 source?
questions.solution: The specification sets a literature fiction text from the 20th or 21st century: an extract from a novel or a short story. The non-fiction sources belong to Paper 2.

markScheme.description: Prose fiction from the 20th or 21st century, such as an extract from a novel or short story

options: Non-fiction from the 19th century, such as a letter, a diary or an extract from a memoir or a travel book
A poem from any century, printed in full
Prose fiction from the 20th or 21st century, such as an extract from a novel or short story
A play script from the 20th century, with stage directions

questions.prompt: What is the technique called when a comparison is made using like or as, such as the lizards darting like flames?
questions.solution: A simile: a comparison made with *like* or *as*. The June 2024 mark scheme built its whole ladder for Question 2 on one, the heat lizards darting over the rocks like flames.

markScheme.description: simile

questions.prompt: A student answering Question 1 writes a point from line 12 when the question asked for lines 1 to 6. What happens?
questions.solution: The mark scheme says responses must be drawn only from the given lines. A true point from elsewhere in the text earns nothing, and the other three points are marked as normal.

markScheme.description: The point earns nothing, because a Question 1 point must come from the given lines only

options: The point earns half a mark, because it is partly right
The whole answer is marked out of 3 instead of 4
The point earns the mark, because it is true and about the subject, and the examiners do not check line numbers
The point earns nothing, because a Question 1 point must come from the given lines only

questions.prompt: What are the three bullets the paper prints under Question 2?
questions.solution: The three bullets are the writer's choice of words and phrases, language features and techniques, and sentence forms. Sentence forms is the bullet most answers forget, and it is a choice like any other.

markScheme.description: Words and phrases; language features and techniques; sentence forms

options: Words and phrases; language features and techniques; sentence forms
Similes; metaphors; personification; and other imagery
Characters; setting; atmosphere; and the narrative voice of the extract
Beginning; middle; end; and the effect of the whole

questions.prompt: A comment says: the word flames tells us the rocks were hot. Which level is that, and why?
questions.solution: The June 2024 scheme gives almost exactly this comment as its Level 1 example: the word tells us they were hot. A Level 3 comment would explain what the image suggests about the heat; a Level 4 comment would read the transformation into fire and its effect on the reader's sense of the character.

markScheme.description: Level 1, because it offers a simple comment on what the word means and goes no further

options: Level 3, because it explains the effect of the writer's choice clearly and uses the word flames as evidence
Level 1, because it offers a simple comment on what the word means and goes no further
Level 4, because it selects a judicious detail
Level 2, because it uses the technical term flames

questions.prompt: What does the opening sentence of Miss Brill do by running through the sky, the light and the gardens before reaching her decision about the fur?
questions.solution: The long sentence, held open by dashes, does what the afternoon does: it takes its time. A sentence-form comment names the shape and says what it does, and this one does the mood of the whole opening.

markScheme.description: It makes the sentence wander the way the afternoon does, so the reader arrives at the fur the way she does, by way of everything else

options: It shows that the writer is more interested in the weather than in the character
It delays the main clause because the sentence is badly constructed
It makes the sentence wander the way the afternoon does, so the reader arrives at the fur the way she does, by way of everything else
It lists the three things the reader needs to know about the setting in order of importance, from the sky down to the gardens and then to the woman herself

questions.prompt: What is the term for the technique in which the fur is given dim little eyes that ask what has been happening to me?
questions.solution: Personification: an object given the qualities of a living thing. The fur has eyes, a life to be rubbed back, and a voice. The term earns when it is used to explain what the choice does: the fur becomes a companion.

markScheme.description: personification

questions.prompt: Put the four moves of a Level 4 paragraph in the order the lesson gives them.
questions.solution: Choose, name, effect, why. The fourth move is the one that turns explanation into analysis, and it is the one most answers stop before.

markScheme.description: the four moves in order

items: Choose a judicious detail that answers the question
Name the choice in exact terms
Give the effect on the reader
Say why the words themselves produce that effect

questions.prompt: Why did the June 2024 mark scheme reject the point she was tired for Question 1, when the text said her head ached and her limbs were heavy?
questions.solution: Question 1 rewards what is in the lines. Her head ached and her limbs were heavy are there; that she was tired is a guess from them. The scheme lists it under reject, with *dehydrated* beside it.

markScheme.description: Because it is an inference the given lines do not make: aching and heaviness are stated, tiredness is not

options: Because tired is too short to count as a point
Because a Question 1 point must be a direct quotation from the given lines and the word tired does not appear anywhere in the text
Because the point is about the setting rather than about Mary
Because it is an inference the given lines do not make: aching and heaviness are stated, tiredness is not

questions.prompt: A student writes a Question 2 answer entirely about a striking metaphor from the last paragraph of the source, outside the lines the question gave. What does the mark scheme say?
questions.solution: The scheme's note is exact: if a student writes only about language outside the given lines, the response is placed in Level 1 or Level 2 according to the quality of what is written. The best analysis on the paper cannot climb above 4 marks from outside the lines.

markScheme.description: The response is placed in Level 1 or Level 2 according to its quality, whatever its insight

options: The response is placed in Level 1 or Level 2 according to its quality, whatever its insight
The response is moved to Question 3, where the whole text counts
The response is marked as normal, because the whole source is available to the student and any part of it can be analysed
The response earns zero, because nothing outside the lines can be credited

questions.prompt: Which of these is sophisticated and accurate terminology in the sense the Level 4 descriptor means?
questions.solution: A term is sophisticated when it names a choice the reader would otherwise miss, and accurate when it is right. Free indirect style, used to explain an effect, is both. Labelling parts of speech, praising vocabulary and spotting alliteration that does nothing are not.

markScheme.description: Free indirect style, used to explain how Little rogue! lets the character's own voice break into the narration

options: Adjectives and nouns, listed for each phrase quoted so that every word in the passage is labelled with its part of speech

questions.prompt: The Level 4 descriptor for Question 2 asks for a range of textual detail chosen with judgement. What is the single word the descriptor uses?
questions.solution: Judicious: selects a range of judicious textual detail. It means chosen with judgement for the question and for how the details connect, not the three things found soonest.

markScheme.description: judicious

questions.prompt: The passage for Question 2 is about a character's loneliness. A student chooses the fur's dim little eyes and Dear little thing! together. Why is that a judicious pair?
questions.solution: The two details make one point in two ways: an object treated as a living thing, and the character's own voice speaking to it. A pair that builds an idea earns more than two unconnected observations, and it answers the question's focus directly.

markScheme.description: Both make the fur a companion, so the two details build one idea about the character in two ways

options: Both are in the first paragraph, which is the part of the passage the examiners read most carefully
Both are short, so they can be quoted quickly and leave time for other questions
Both make the fur a companion, so the two details build one idea about the character in two ways
Both contain the word little, so the student can write about repetition

questions.prompt: How does the writer use language to show how Miss Brill feels about her fur? Write one Level 4 paragraph on this sentence from the opening: “She had taken it out of its box that afternoon, shaken out the moth-powder, given it a good brush, and rubbed the life back into the dim little eyes.” Name the choices, give their effects, and say why the words produce them.
questions.solution: Mansfield builds the sentence as a list of small, careful actions, taken out, shaken, brushed, rubbed, and the list form itself is a choice: it makes the reader watch a ritual, each step given its own clause, so that the fur is handled with the attention a person might give to a child or a pet being got ready. The verbs are domestic and gentle, and the last of them, *rubbed the life back*, is what one does to a numb hand or a chilled animal, so the fur is not simply cleaned but revived, and the reader understands that this is something Miss Brill brings back to life each Sunday. The eyes, *dim* until she attends to them and then *little*, are personified twice over: the adjective gives them a state that can change, and the diminutive gives them the affection of a name. The effect is of a woman whose tenderness has nowhere else to go, and the reader feels that before the story has said a word about her loneliness. The sentence form finishes the work: the long sentence ends on the eyes, so that the fur looks back at her, and at us, as the paragraph turns to what those eyes say.

questions.prompt: How does the writer use language in the second paragraph of the extract, from There were a number of people to she lifted her head and smiled, to show what the afternoon means to Miss Brill? Write a full Question 2 answer of about the length you would write in the exam.
questions.solution: The paragraph shows the afternoon through what Miss Brill notices, and every detail is chosen to reveal how much it means to her. The band, she thinks, sounds louder and gayer because the Season has begun, and Mansfield gives the reason in her own reasoning: out of season the band was like someone playing with only the family to listen, an image that makes the music a performance for strangers and makes Miss Brill one of the strangers it is for. The question she asks herself, whether the conductor is wearing a new coat, is a sentence form that puts the reader inside her attention, and the answer, that she was sure it was new, shows how carefully she watches. The conductor scraping his foot and flapping his arms like a rooster about to crow is a simile that is affectionate and faintly comic at once, so the reader shares her pleasure in watching people. Then the music arrives as a little chain of bright drops, an image of something small, pretty and precious, and the exclamation *very pretty!* is her voice again. The short final sentence, that she lifted her head and smiled, is the effect of all of it: the afternoon gives her a place, an audience to belong to and something to expect, and the reader watches her receive it.

questions.prompt: A student writes: Mansfield uses lots of adjectives and similes to make the description vivid. Why does this comment sit in the lower levels however true it is?
questions.solution: The scheme rewards analysis of the effects of the writer's choices. A sentence that says adjectives and similes make things vivid could be written about any passage ever printed. Naming is Level 1 or 2; effect is Level 3; why the words produce it is Level 4.

options: It mentions the writer by her surname alone, which the mark scheme says examiners should treat as a discourtesy and mark down
It uses the word vivid, which examiners regard as a banned word
It is too short, because the mark scheme says that a Level 3 answer to Question 2 must run to at least a full page of the answer booklet, and this comment is one sentence long
It names techniques without saying what any one of them does to the reader, which is the difference between labelling and analysing

questions.prompt: For Question 1, a student writes: Miss Brill was glad she had decided on her fur, and she had taken it out of its box and brushed it. How is this marked?
questions.solution: The scheme says any response that combines two or more correct points should be awarded the appropriate mark, and gives an example of one line earning three. Two true things about the subject from the given lines are two marks, whatever the punctuation between them.

markScheme.description: As two points, each earning a mark, because the scheme awards the appropriate mark to a response that combines correct points

options: As two points, each earning a mark, because the scheme awards the appropriate mark to a response that combines correct points
As one point plus a bonus for using a quotation
As one point, because the answer is written as a single sentence and the mark scheme says that one sentence can only ever earn one mark, however many things it says
As nothing, because Question 1 answers must be single words written on the numbered lines, and a full sentence breaks that rule and is not marked

examTechnique.body:
**Read first.** About 15 minutes on the source and all five questions. Two reads, the second with a pencil.

**Question 1 is exactness.** Four separate true things about the named subject from the given lines only. A word will do. No inference the lines do not make: *tired* and *dehydrated* were rejected in June 2024 when the text said her head ached and she wanted water.

**Question 2 is depth on a few details.** Stay inside the given lines. Choose two or three judicious details that answer the question's focus and connect. For each: name the choice, give the effect on the reader, say why the words produce it. Cover a sentence form as well as words and images.

**Terminology earns when it explains.** Personification, free indirect style, exclamatory sentence: used to name a choice the reader would otherwise miss. *Adjectives* and *powerful vocabulary* earn nothing.

**Time.** A few minutes for Question 1, about ten for Question 2, and on to the eight marks of Question 3.
examinerErrors: Answering Question 1 from outside the given lines, or with an inference the lines do not make.
Writing about the setting when Question 1 asked about a person.
Naming techniques without any effect: the writer uses similes and adjectives to make it vivid.
Writing a Question 2 answer about language outside the given lines, which caps the response at Level 2.
Ignoring sentence forms, the third bullet under the question.
Spending twenty minutes on the eight marks of Question 2 and running out of time for the twenty marks of Question 4.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer to Question 1 is four plain, separate, true points from the lines given, written in a couple of minutes. To Question 2 it is two or three details chosen because they answer the question and connect, each named in exact terms, each given an effect on the reader, and each explained through the words themselves: the verb phrase that revives the fur, the exclamation that lets her voice in, the sentence that corrects itself. It includes a sentence form among its choices, stays inside the lines, and reads the details together as one idea about the passage rather than as a list of techniques.
